mcqs.question: When answering "where are the single points of failure in this design," what's the strongest approach?
options: Walk every component in the diagram and flag any with a count of one, not just the obvious one
Name the database, since it's almost always the SPOF that matters most
Assume any component sitting behind a load balancer is automatically safe from being a SPOF
Wait for the interviewer to point out which components to check
mcqs.explanation: A systematic scan of every component catches the SPOFs that get missed — the load balancer itself, a shared internal dependency — not just the database everyone remembers to name. A load balancer sitting in front of replicated servers is itself often unreplicated, so it isn't automatically safe.

mcqs.question: A database primary fails over to a standby replica automatically. What real cost should you name alongside this fix?
options: There is no cost — automated failover is a completely lossless operation
Some recent writes that hadn't replicated to the standby before the failure may be lost — a real RPO
The fix only works if the database has no write traffic at all
Automated failover eliminates the need for any read replicas going forward
mcqs.explanation: Failover to a standby has a real recovery point objective — writes acknowledged by the primary but not yet replicated at the moment of failure are gone. It isn't lossless, doesn't require zero write traffic, and doesn't remove the separate need for read replicas.

mcqs.question: You've added automated failover for your database primary, detected and triggered by a single health-check daemon. What have you actually achieved?
options: You've fully eliminated the single point of failure with no remaining risk
You've made the system slower without improving its resilience at all
You've moved the single point of failure one layer — the health-check daemon itself is now a SPOF for triggering failover
You've introduced a security vulnerability unrelated to availability
mcqs.explanation: If the coordinator that detects failure and promotes the replica is itself a single instance, it's now the thing that has to survive for failover to work at all — the SPOF didn't disappear, it relocated. This isn't a security issue, and it does meaningfully improve resilience for the original failure mode even though a new one appears.

mcqs.question: A candidate names the database as the only single point of failure in a system that also has one load balancer and one shared auth service every request depends on. What's missing?
options: Nothing — the database is always the most important SPOF to name
A discussion of the database's specific storage engine
Recognizing that the load balancer and the shared auth service are just as much single points of failure, and are commonly missed
mcqs.explanation: Any unreplicated component on the critical path is a SPOF — the load balancer and a shared auth dependency qualify just as much as the database, and are the ones most often overlooked. Storage engine details and ACID properties aren't what this question is probing.
